title: The two Jalals
hookLine: a short, classic commentary written by two scholars named Jalal al-Din
tomorrow: you've got the commentaries. so who do you ask?

lines: A FEW WORDS BESIDE THE VERSE.
cards: A recipe online sometimes makes you scroll past a long life story before the ingredients. Some days you want the story. Some days you just need two cups and medium heat.
When you're new to a hard text, how much help is enough? Here's this path's answer, in a book: the Tafsir al-Jalalayn, the commentary of the two Jalals.
It's the two-cups kind, a few words at a time, tucked right beside the verse.

teach.b: Two scholars named Jalal al-Din wrote it. Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli began it; after his death, Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti completed it, and says so.

teach.h: A WORD, A NAME, A QUICK NOTE.
teach.b: Their way is short and clear: a hard word glossed, a pronoun named, a quick note on context, often in a phrase woven into the line of the verse itself. You read the Qur'an and its plain sense almost in one breath.
The big commentaries of this week are rooms you can live in. This one is a doorway, and a learner needs a doorway first. Here's a neighbor who answers the same question in his own words.
Rashi, the Jewish commentator on the Torah, writes in his note on Genesis that he has come only for the plain meaning of scripture, the peshat, and for those teachings that settle its words.
Jewish learners have long studied the Torah with his brief notes beside it. Shared ground: help a learner see the plain meaning first, in as few words as it takes. And one honest difference.
They serve different scriptures, held in different ways: for Jews, the Torah, read with the Talmud and the rabbis; for Muslims, the Qur'an, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
Two traditions, each starting the learner at the door.

how: Students of tafsir often begin with the Jalalayn, reading it with a teacher verse by verse; it is printed in the margins of some editions of the Qur'an.

games.q: at bedtime your little cousin asks what a hard verse means. what fits the two Jalals?
o: the plain meaning, in a sentence or two; deeper can wait.
every view the scholars hold on it, so she gets it right.
tell her she's too young for that verse for now.
games.why: short and clear: a doorway first. the big commentaries are still there when she's ready.

practice: Count three things you're grateful for today on your fingers, one word each. No explanations, no stories, just the word. Then sit quietly with the three words, short and clear, and let them be enough for now.

wordCard.voice: The two Jalals: al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti, whose short commentary, the Jalalayn, gives a few clear words beside each verse.

orig.note: Arabic: al-Jalalayn, the two Jalals; the name of their commentary.

carryVoice: To take with you: short and clear, a doorway before the rooms. Commentators, five of six.
